common_name: Pink Spire Summersweet (Historic Non-Fading Pink Clethra)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Pink Spire is a long-cultivated selection, first named in 1906, valued for light pink flowers that hold their color rather than fading toward white as the spikes age.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, though it tolerates a half-day of sun with steady moisture; summersweet flowers most heavily with at least some sun but performs reliably in shadier spots where few other flowering shrubs bloom well. Pink Spire is one of the oldest named cultivars of the native Eastern summersweet, selected in 1906 for its clear, light pink flower spikes that resist the fading to near-white seen in some other pink selections as the bottlebrush-shaped blooms age through midsummer. Its intense, spicy-sweet fragrance carries widely and draws heavy bee and butterfly traffic during a season when many spring shrubs have already finished flowering. Like other summersweet selections it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil far better than most shrubs and spreads slowly by suckers, making it useful for a damp, shaded border, rain garden, or naturalized planting.
sources: Native Plant Trust Go Botany / Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Sherry Sue is grown as much for its pinkish-red new stems, visible through the dormant season, as for its fragrant summer flowers.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Sherry Sue tolerates heavy clay and periodically saturated soil better than most shrubs, and shade actually improves its most distinctive feature. New stem growth emerges a striking pinkish-red and holds that color through the season and into winter, giving this slow-growing, upright selection of native summersweet a second season of interest well beyond its mid-to-late-summer spikes of intensely fragrant pink-and-white flowers. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the blooms heavily, and the dark green foliage provides a clean backdrop for the colored stems. It suckers gently to form a slowly expanding colony over time; remove unwanted suckers each spring if a tighter, single-clump form is preferred.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Rosealind is a compact Deutzia x elegantissima hybrid grown for its unusually deep rose-pink flower color compared to the pastel pinks of most deutzia.

directions: Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Rosealind tolerates a range of soil types including clay and chalk once established and needs little supplemental water beyond its first season. This compact, rounded hybrid deutzia bears dense clusters of star-shaped, deep rosy-pink flowers in late spring to early summer, a noticeably richer, more saturated pink than the pale blush tones typical of many deutzia hybrids, on a shrub that stays smaller and tidier than most Deutzia x hybrida selections. Prune immediately after flowering, thinning out some of the oldest stems at the base, since Rosealind blooms on the previous year's wood and later pruning sacrifices next year's display. It is a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a mixed border or foundation planting where a compact deutzia with unusually strong flower color is wanted.

common_name: Manteau d'Hermine Mock Orange (Dwarf Double-Flowered Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf, French Lemoine-bred mock orange stays under 3 feet tall, far smaller than most mock orange cultivars, making it suitable for small gardens and large containers.

directions: Manteau d'Hermine is a dwarf mock orange bred in the late 1800s by French hybridizer Victor Lemoine, prized for its compact, fountain-shaped habit that stays under 3 feet tall at maturity, far smaller than the 6-to-10-foot mounds typical of most mock orange shrubs. In late spring to early summer, arching branches carry small clusters of fully double, creamy-white flowers with an intense, sweet fragrance that belies the plant's diminutive size. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune immediately after flowering, removing a few of the oldest stems at the base, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes next year's flowers. Its small mature size and tolerance of light shade make it a good fit for foundation plantings, small borders, or large containers where full-size mock orange cultivars would quickly outgrow the space.
